body:
Is there any MRP/example for what this would fix (i use openSUSE as my main OS and could test it)? AFAICT this would work for loading dynamic libraries from `$binary_directory/../lib` and `../lib64` but the fact that `lib64` is needed makes me think that what this PR is trying to do is load libraries from the system global directories (since `lib64` is something that has to do with a distro) - the current code only looks into directories relative to the binary.

It would work for a binary placed in, say, `/usr/bin` to find a library in `/usr/lib64` but a binary in `/usr/local/bin` wouldn't find a library in `/usr/lib64`. If that is the requirement then i think instead of adding an extra check for `lib64` perhaps a better approach would be to make an attempt to open the given file with `dlopen` right before the `ERR_FAIL_COND_V(!FileAccess::exists(path), ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND);` check and, if that succeeds, to use `dlinfo` to find the directory that contains the given file to fill `p_data->r_resolved_path`. This would need some OS-specific `#ifdef`s since `dlinfo` is only available on Linux and some BSDs and not all BSDs support the same queries, but it should still be better than the current approach.

Sure, I'm all for an even more robust approach if that's what the maintainers want, but this PR was just a simple extension to the existing approach which like you said would make the binary in e.g. `/usr/bin` search for `/usr/lib64` or for `/usr/local/bin` in `/usr/local/lib64` instead of just `lib`.

I tried my hand at implementing the suggestion from @badsectoracula. I am unsure if everything especially for BSD is correct, I only tested it to work as expected on linux so testing and feedback is very welcome :slightly_smiling_face:

Do we really want to load GDExtensions from system paths? Are folks actually installing their `libmyextension.linux.template_debug.x86_64.so` into `/usr/lib`?

Given that GDExtensions have a nuanced compatibility relationship with the version of Godot you're using, and you can't really distribute a `.gdextension` file that assumes the user has something installed in a system lib path, I'm not sure this is a feature we want to support.

The existing `OS_Unix::open_dynamic_library()` code does have a branch that appears aimed at loading from system `lib` directories, but I'd love to hear from folks who are depending on this feature - what is your use case for this?

`open_dynamic_library()` isn't only used for loading GDExtensions, and I could definitely see an argument for loading system libraries with it, but we know from the 3rd argument if it's being used for GDExtension or not, and we could reserve that feature for when _not_ loading a GDExtension.

> The existing `OS_Unix::open_dynamic_library()` code does have a branch that appears aimed at loading from system `lib` directories, but I'd love to hear from folks who are depending on this feature - what is your use case for this?

My use case is an app that uses a gdextension library. I wanted to create an rpm package for that app and stumbled upon the issue I described, where it doesn't load `lib64`.
Personally I do like the approach to try to load from configured system paths instead of just hardcoded paths, but if it's preferred to use the existing approach and extend it with `../lib64` I can of course also change it back.

> My use case is an app that uses a gdextension library. I wanted to create an rpm package for that app and stumbled upon the issue I described, where it doesn't load `lib64`.

What is the GDExtension library? Is it a commonly used one that other apps may use too?

I guess what I'm getting at, is what happens if you have two apps and they both depend on the same GDExtension library, but different versions of it (potentially because they were built with different versions of Godot)?

In the case of all Open Source apps, I guess you could modify both apps to work with the same version of Godot and the GDExtension library, but this still feels like a kind of delicate situation. Games are frequently very tightly bound to the Godot and GDExtension versions they were built for.

> What is the GDExtension library? Is it a commonly used one that other apps may use too?

Maybe? Currently definitely not, because I wrote it for the app, but still the right location for this library is in `/usr/lib64` when it is being installed at a system level.

> I guess what I'm getting at, is what happens if you have two apps and they both depend on the same GDExtension library, but different versions of it (potentially because they were built with different versions of Godot)?

Well godot certainly isn't the first to have this issue, that's why libraries are supposed to be versioned with their SONAME. I don't think this needs to be solved here.

"Entry"/"Main" gdextensions don't really make sense to load from system paths (as they only really make sense with the rest of the pck and template).
Library GDExtensions are not depended upon, they are vendored and bundled into the final zip so I wouldn't put pressure on distro maintainers to package even more things that they already do.

If someday there is real package management in godot (not just vendoring dependencies and calling it a day) then maybe this could be revisited by having some compatibility between godot packages and linux packages (or not seeing as the theoretical package manager could place these libraries anywhere at all like nuget and cargo do, entirely sidestepping the system manager).

At the end of the day even as someone who maintains a highly de-vendored version of godot for local dev, the godot model is not about executables and dependencies. It is about executables with vendored dependencies which do not play well with a package managed model.

As for `$ORIGIN/../lib` I say we could keep it. Someone could distrubute a zip with the executable `./bin` and the gdextension in `./lib` . When installing things the separation might be useful and it also allows for paths like `~/.local/bin` and `~/.local/lib` to function without putting dynamic libraries in the PATH
If it isn't intended to share gdextension library files anyway, maybe it should just statically link the whole binary.

> If it isn't intended to share gdextension library files anyway, maybe it should just statically link the whole binary.

The reason we use shared libraries is purely practical: it allows users to download and use a single Godot executable, and then in their individual projects, download (or create) GDExtensions that expand the functionality of the engine for that project.

In other words, we think of the GDExtensions that a project uses as part of the project. A single copy of a GDExtension is not meant to be used by multiple projects.

When you are distributing your application, if you wanted to statically link all your GDExtensions with the Godot executeable, that absolutely can make sense! In fact, I think that might be what we do by default when exporting to iOS? I'm not totally sure about that, though :-)

Side note: We have been talking about adding the concept of "global GDExtensions". But the idea is that those would only extend the functionality of the Godot editor - not all projects that are using Godot - and they would probably be specific to the Godot editor version (so you'd have a set of global extensions for Godot 4.2, a different set for 4.3, etc)

Regarding prior art in Linux distribution packages, the closest equivalent are open source games based on various id Tech engines (e.g. Warsow, OpenArena). Game logic (and mods) are shipped with DLL/SO files that part of the same folder as the game data, despite being executable code. These are not packaged separately from the rest of the game data, since there is no expectation that you'll be loading those DLLs externally.

GDExtension follows a similar usability model, so I don't think there is much point in attempting to load them from system paths.

For games I totally agree, however at least to my understanding godot also tries to, at least to some extent, support other applications and in that case a data directory really isn't the standard.

I guess another way this could maybe also be solved is by giving the developer more control over where a library is loaded from, because right now AFAICT it is pretty limited. Unless I am missing something I can only specify a path in the `.gdextension` file and can't without hackery change it dynamically at runtime, right?

If you want to compare it against other open source games, I just looked at 0ad for openSUSE. The way they do it is by adding the shared libraries inside `/usr/lib64/0ad` and then there is a sort of compile time argument that allows to specify the library dir via `--libdir=/usr/lib64/0ad`. Now I would say in theory this "compile time switch" is easy enough in godot by simply running a regex over the `.gdextension` files before exporting. ~~However this still wouldn't actually work, because only relative paths to either the CWD or the binary are supported. Is the support for absolute paths at least something I could add?~~
Edit: Oops, I am wrong, absolute paths are supported :slightly_smiling_face:. Okay then I am fine with closing this PR, since I have found a workaround that works for me.

Actually, one can't really regex the `.gdextension` files before export, because then the export fails unless it already is at that path on the host system. I mean it still results in a valid binary, just without the library files copied to the export dir. I guess I can technically just ignore this failure and copy the library files myself. I think I could also change the path in the exported binary with some hackery, but all of these are IMO really ugly workarounds *sigh*.

I definitely think there is room for improvement for the gdextension library path handling, but tbh I've had enough of this topic for now.
